proposals.description: Telemetry shows a sustained, progressive rise in coolant temp from 90°C to 114°C over ~2 hours, paired with a steady drop in coolant level from 96% to 76% — not a brief transient. Oil pressure and RPM remain stable, ruling out broader engine failure. KB has two conflicting entries: KB-001 attributes spikes to a sensor calibration glitch (fix: restart_sensor), while KB-002 links sustained spikes correlated with falling coolant level to a genuine leak (fix: schedule_service_visit). The data clearly matches KB-002's pattern (correlated, sustained, non-transient), so despite the conflict I favor the more cautious option of physical inspection rather than assuming a sensor fault.

Telemetry shows a sustained, monotonic coolant temp rise (90°C→114°C over 2 hours) tightly correlated with a steady coolant level drop (96%→76%), while oil pressure and RPM stayed stable — this matches KB-002's pattern of genuine coolant loss/leak, not a transient sensor artifact. Note: KB-001 and KB-002 disagree on root cause for 'coolant temp spike' (sensor glitch vs. real leak); given the correlated level drop and sustained (non-transient) nature here, KB-002 fits better and is the more cautious choice given last coolant service was 3+ months ago (2026-06-02). Recommend physical inspection/service visit rather than a simple sensor restart, to avoid overheating/engine damage from an unaddressed leak.

Telemetry shows cabin_temp_c climbing steadily from ~2°C to 5.8°C over 3 hours while controller_reading_c stays oscillating tightly around the 2°C setpoint (1.8-2.2°C) — the controller "believes" it is holding setpoint even as the cabin diverges, and compressor current is actually tapering off (11.1A→8.5A), confirming the controller is under-cooling based on a stale/miscalibrated sensor reading rather than actual cabin conditions. This matches KB-003's documented pattern for controller sensor calibration drift, for which the fix is a diagnostic reset to re-run self-calibration. KB-003 explicitly excludes this fix when controller reading tracks the cabin probe (that would indicate a refrigeration circuit fault needing a technician instead) — here the two readings clearly diverge, so the diagnostic-reset branch applies. No conflicting KB entries were found and no prior service history exists for this unit.

This matches KB-003's documented pattern for controller sensor calibration drift (controller reading tracks setpoint, not actual cabin temp), for which the fix is a remote diagnostic reset to re-run self-calibration. KB-003 explicitly states this fix does not apply if controller reading tracks the cabin probe instead — which is not the case here, so no conflict applies. Service history has no prior related visits. Confidence is 0.85 given the clean match to the documented KB pattern.

proposals.description: Telemetry shows stable operation (~11-12A) until 20:10, when compressor_current_a spiked to 24A, then collapsed to 0A with compressor_state flipping to "fault" at 20:20 and remaining there through the end of the window. Cabin temp has since risen steadily from 2.0°C to 4.8°C, above the 2°C setpoint, with controller_reading_c tracking cabin_temp_c exactly at every sample (no divergence). KB-003 (temperature drift) explicitly states that a diagnostic reset only applies when the controller reading diverges from the cabin probe (sensor calibration drift); when the controller tracks the cabin probe as it does here, the refrigeration circuit itself is at fault and requires a technician. Combined with the overcurrent spike and sustained fault state (consistent with a compressor trip, not a sensor issue), this points to a real mechanical/electrical compressor fault rather than a software/calibration issue. No other KB entries or service history exist to contradict this, so recommending a service visit as the cautious option rather than a remote reset.
